questions.q: How are elements in a list accessed?
options: Lists cannot be accessed at all once created
Only by iterating from the beginning every time
By position, using a zero-based index
By a named key, like a dictionary
questions.explain: fare_amounts[0] gets the first element; fare_amounts[-1] gets the last.

questions.q: How are values in a dictionary accessed?
options: Only by numeric index, like a list
By a named key, not by position
By alphabetical order automatically
Dictionaries cannot store more than one value
questions.explain: trip['fare_amount'] retrieves the value associated with that specific key.

questions.q: What does it mean that lists are mutable?
options: Lists can only hold one data type at a time
A list's contents can never change once created
Elements can be added, removed, or changed after the list is created
Mutable means the list is stored on disk instead of memory
questions.explain: .append() is a direct example of mutating a list after creation.

questions.q: Why does a Python dictionary look structurally identical to a JSON object?
options: Dictionaries can only be used with XML, not JSON
Because Lesson 24's JSON processing reads a JSON object and hands back exactly this kind of Python dictionary automatically
JSON objects are actually a completely different data structure
It's a coincidence with no real connection
questions.explain: This structural match is exactly why JSON parses so naturally into Python's native data types.

questions.q: What does a list of dictionaries represent, conceptually?
options: A dictionary that has been converted into a string
A type of error in Python
A single value with no internal structure
Something that looks like rows in a table, each dictionary representing one row
questions.explain: This is exactly the shape Lesson 22 gets from reading a JSON file, and what a Pandas DataFrame formalizes further.
